Read it: the whole generator body sits inside a `try` (deliberately, because a generator function runs none of its body until iterated — a `try` around the request alone would never see a connect failure), and that outer try has `catch (HttpException $e)` and `catch (GuzzleException $e)`, the latter rethrowing as `new HttpException('Stream from ... failed: ' . ..., 0, '', $e)`. #SO THE DEFECT IS SOUND IN SQL SEMANTICS AND UNPROVEN IN OBSERVATION, and those are different claims. The outer `ORDER BY` on a single-row aggregate really is inert as SQL goes, and moving it into the derived table really is the correct form. But this fixture cannot tell the two apart, because SQLite's plan for THIS query happens to feed the aggregate in a usable order regardless. A test that passes on the broken code is not a regression test, and calling it one would be the exact failure this loop has spent 146 iterations refusing — a guard that cannot fail, reported as proof.

#The honest way to make it observable is to force the two orders apart at the STORAGE layer rather than at the read: insert rows in a physical order the optimiser can exploit differently, or assert against a query whose plan is known. Until such a fixture exists, the fix is a CORRECTNESS IMPROVEMENT argued from the language spec, not a measured repair, and the ledger says so rather than implying the deferral is nearly done.

#THE TEST IS KEPT as a characterisation test: it pins the behaviour actually promised and will fail loudly if the pending-write order ever regresses, whatever the plan. It is deliberately NOT claimed as the mutation that proves the fix, because it does not.

#THE API SHAPES ARE RECORDED so the next iteration does not repeat the guess: `putWrites(array $config, array $writes, string $taskId): array`; writes are `[['channel','value'],...]`; `getTuple($config)` returns a tuple whose `pendingWrites` is a list of `[taskId, channel, value]`. Not a malformed block: a FATAL. mergeContent(null, null) and mergeContent([...blocks], null) both threw 'ContentBlock::text(): Argument #1 ($text) must be of type string, null given'. Upstream reaches its final else for a null second side and returns [...left, {type:'text', text: secondContent}] — a text block whose text is null, no error, because contentBlocksFromNonStringFirst(null) returns []. The port now normalises a null side to '' before anything else, so the merge works and only the unrepresentable text:null is lost. Null is unreachable through the message classes — AIMessageChunk coerces content:null to [] — so this fires only when a caller passes null to this PUBLIC method. That is what separates it from the Completions::encode() landmine: a private method nothing can reach is a hazard, a public method a caller can invoke is an interface. [];` then `existing.push(resume);` then `yield [tid, RESUME, existing];`. The port does exactly that: IO.php:183-190 collects the matching prior RESUME writes, `$existing = array_slice($existing, 0, 1);`, `$existing[] = $value;`, then yields. The reviewer suggested 'if the intent is replacement, remove the append logic entirely' — upstream keeps the append, after truncating to the single most recent value. And the code comment already said so, citing io.ts:108, and explained that it was PREVIOUSLY documented the other way round, which is what invited the finding. So this was a duplicate report against code that already carried the receipt, and the deferral is now closed with the quote rather than left as a standing question.
google/gemini-3.1-pro-preview: #1 MAJOR 'a callable partial returning an array is cast to the string "Array"' — ACCEPTED, measured, and worse as described. The cast was (is_callable($value) ? (string) $value() : $value). With a partial returning ['A','B'], the merge produced the literal string "Array" and the template rendered 'FArray', with a PHP warning on top — and under failOnWarning="true" that warning is also a failure. Upstream assigns it UNCAST: base.ts:112-117 does `partialValues[key] = await (value as () => Promise<string>)();`. So the cast was an addition rather than a translation of that line, and it laundered the caller's value into a word. Upstream's declared type is string-valued, so the ordinary case is identical and is pinned separately; removing the cast makes the out-of-contract case visible instead of silently wrong. After: 'F["A","B"]'. Mutation-verified.

#2 MAJOR 'tuple-style chat templates crash on content blocks' — REJECTED by execution. ChatPromptTemplate::fromMessages([['human', [['type'=>'text','text'=>'hi']]]]) rendered [{"type":"text","text":"hi"}] with no TypeError. The cited path does not reach a string-only signature for array content.

#3 MAJOR 'non-array inputs are silently discarded' — REJECTED on the contract. invoke('World') does throw PromptInputError: Missing value for input variable `name`, so the behaviour described is real — but upstream's formatPromptValue is ABSTRACT and documented as taking 'A dictionary of arguments to be passed to the prompt template' (base.ts:151-153), and invoke() forwards input to it unchanged (base.ts:143). So a bare string is outside the contract upstream too. Throwing InvalidArgumentError instead of the current error would be a different message for the same unsupported input, not a fix.

#4 MINOR 'image_url array without a url key loses its detail configuration' — DEFERRED with a reason, not accepted: it needs a reachable input shape (an image_url carrying 'detail' but no 'url') and a decision about whether such a block is meaningful at all, since the whole point of the branch is formatting a URL template. Not verifiable cheaply, so not acted on in a review iteration.
google/gemini-3.1-pro-preview-customtool: #1 BLOCKER 'PartialJsonParser crashes on UTF-16 surrogate pairs' — ACCEPTED, and the worst defect found in a while. mb_chr((int) hexdec($hex), 'UTF-8') returns false for a surrogate code point (measured: mb_chr(0xD83D,'UTF-8') === false), and the method is typed string, so ANY emoji in a streamed JSON response died with `TypeError: parseUnicodeEscape(): Return value must be of type string, false returned`. Measured on new PartialJsonParser('"\\uD83D\\uDE00"'). Upstream never hits it because String.fromCharCode (utils/json.ts:86) returns the lone surrogate and JS strings hold surrogate code units natively; the two halves render as the character. PHP's mbstring is stricter and CORRECT, so the port reassembles the pair into the scalar it stands for. Verified by bytes: emoji -> f09f9880 (U+1F600), CJK U+20BB7 -> f0a0aeb7, 'a😀b' -> 3 chars, lone surrogate -> U+FFFD rather than fataling. Mutation-verified (restoring the bare mb_chr reproduces the TypeError).

#2 MAJOR 'format instructions contain literal backslashes' — ACCEPTED, measured. The instruction string was written as \`\`\`json inside a double-quoted PHP literal; PHP has no \` escape, so each backslash survived and str_contains($instructions, "\\`") was TRUE. The model was told to emit a corrupted fence — and since the extractor matches on real fences, that request produces output the parser will not recognise, surfacing much later as an unrelated 'Failed to parse'. Fixed; mutation-verified by putting the backslashes back.

#3 MAJOR 'a bare fence after a preamble is rejected' — REJECTED, and the port is a line-for-line port of upstream. structured.ts:113-115 is: trimmedText.match(/^```(?:json)?\s*([\s\S]*?)```/)?.[1] || trimmedText.match(/```json\s*([\s\S]*?)```/)?.[1] || trimmedText. The same two patterns, in the same order, with the second requiring `json` exactly as the port does. Measured: 'preamble + bare fence' throws OutputParserException while 'bare fence at start' parses — and upstream does the same. Making `json` optional in the second pattern would diverge and change which model outputs parse.

#process a failed python write DESTROYED a source file mid-iteration. The patch text contained a literal \uD83D inside a non-raw python string, python decoded it as a surrogate, and open(path,'w') had ALREADY truncated the file before the encode error fired — PartialJsonParser.php went to 0 bytes and the class vanished from the autoloader. Recovered only because it was committed. The lesson is the mirror of the silent-success edit this project already tracks: open(path,'w') is destructive before it is successful, so writes now go to a temp file and os.replace() into position, and the patch text lives in its own file rather than inside an escaping sandwich.
deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp: #1 MAJOR 'an empty {} argument object is rejected by an object schema' — ACCEPTED, measured. "arguments": "{}" decodes to [] in PHP, Js::isList([]) is true, so matchesType([], 'object') was false and the type check errored BEFORE the checkSub() disambiguation that exists precisely to resolve this. A tool declared Schema::object(['q'=>Schema::string()]) with nothing required could never be called with no arguments — invoke([]) threw ToolException — and models really do send {}. The ambiguity is now resolved at the type check too, but ONLY where the schema declares object keywords, so `required` is still enforced on an empty object and a bare `type: array` still means a list. Mutation-verified.

#2 MAJOR 'a failure after execute() orphans the tool trace run' — ACCEPTED, measured by reading the guard's extent. callToolWithValidation() wrapped only execute() in try/catch; splitResult() and ToolOutput::format() sat AFTER it, so either failure escaped with no handleToolError and no handleToolEnd — a span open forever, the same shape as the batch-run leak fixed earlier. Both are now inside the guard. Mutation-verified by moving them back out.

#3 MINOR 'allOf short-circuits its siblings' — ACCEPTED, and it FAILS OPEN, which is the serious direction. The allOf branch ended in `return`, so once the clauses held the sibling keywords never ran. Measured on {type:object, properties:{a:{type:string}}, allOf:[{required:[b]}]}: input {a:1, b:'y'} was ACCEPTED with `a` declared a string and holding an integer. An earlier probe of mine MISSED this because {a:'x'} fails the allOf clause first and masked the sibling skip; the tell is {a:1,b:'y'}. Now falls through rather than returning. anyOf still short-circuits, correctly — it is a disjunction. Mutation-verified.

#4 MINOR 'integer rejects the JSON spelling 3.0' — ACCEPTED. JSON Schema 2019-09+ defines integer as a number with zero fractional part, and json_decode('3.0') yields float. Measured: an integer field holding 3.0 was refused with 'expected integer, got number', so a model writing 3.0 had its whole call rejected. Now accepts a finite float equal to floor(). INF is explicitly still not an integer, which is pinned because the new float branch would otherwise launder it. Mutation-verified.

#5 MINOR 'mergeConfig drops a default context' — ACCEPTED. ToolRuntime::fromConfig() reads $config->context (ToolRuntime.php:60) and mergeConfig() copied tags, metadata, callbacks, options, runName and configurable — context was absent, so a defaultConfig carrying a runtime context lost it whenever the caller did not pass one per call. Added a branch mirroring the others. NOTE: my first probe of this reported ToolRuntime returning ABSENT context, which was wrong — fromConfig returns null outright when toolCall is unset, so the probe was measuring a null object. The finding was real; the probe was not.

openai/o4-mini: #4 MINOR 'composer.json does not declare ext-pdo_sqlite though SqliteSaver ships in src/' — ACCEPTED. Measured: require held only ext-json, ext-mbstring, guzzlehttp/guzzle, guzzlehttp/psr7, php, psr/log, ramsey/uuid, and SqliteSaver constructs a PDO against SQLite, so a consumer without the extension got a fatal at the first checkpoint write instead of a message from composer. Declared in require-dev (the suite needs it) and suggest (the saver ships), NOT in require: upstream keeps that saver in a SEPARATE optional package (@langchain/langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite), so a hard requirement would force pdo_sqlite on every consumer for a backend most never touch. My first patch put it in require as well and the new guard caught MY OWN mistake, which is the guard earning its place on the first run.

google/gemini-3.6-flash: #3 MINOR 'StructuredOutput binds run_name instead of camelCase runName' — ACCEPTED, NOT mutation-verified. RunnableConfig reads $runName and upstream's RunnableBinding.kwargs is typed Partial<CallOptions>, where runName is the canonical key, so `run_name` was not a synonym: it landed in config->options['run_name'], runName stayed null, and every named structured-output pipeline showed up unnamed in a trace. A snake_case key that is quietly accepted and quietly ignored is worse than one that is rejected, because nothing reports the loss. Fixed to `runName`. HONEST LABEL: I could not get a regression fixture green — I guessed five signatures wrong (StructuredOutput::run does not exist, DynamicStructuredTool::make does not exist, tool() takes two args not three, the output parser must be a Runnable, and use-function had imported the class as a function) — so the fix ships WITHOUT a test. #2 MAJOR 'a string runId is sliced to its first character' — REJECTED by measurement. RunnableConfig declares `public array $runId = []`, so $config->runId[0] is always an array offset; measured, an array runId yields 'abc' correctly. Passing a string is impossible — the property is typed, so it would be a TypeError at construction. The reviewer's premise ('when runId is a UUID string') describes a state the type system forbids.

#4 MAJOR 'sumOutputs fatals adding non-numeric keys' — REJECTED. BaseChatModel::sumOutputs already guards with `is_int($value) || is_float($value)` before performing the addition, and $base[$key] at that point has only ever been assigned by this same function's numeric branch. #5 MINOR 'the stall guard cannot run because read() blocks' — REJECTED by measurement, and this one challenged a fix I shipped three iterations ago. Measured directly: a blocking socket read with a 1s stream timeout returned after exactly 1.00s with `false`. Guzzle sets `timeout` on the request (GuzzleHttpClient lines 54 and 86), which bounds the read, so a genuinely silent socket returns and the silence check runs. The guard is effective. Worth noting the real nuance rather than the claim: with a read timeout in play, the effective ceiling is whichever of the two fires first, so streamSilenceLimit only matters when it is SHORTER than the read timeout.

#1 MAJOR 'unguarded $generation->message access fatals on non-chat generations' — DEFERRED, not rejected: it is plausible and cheap to fix (wrap the assignment the way stampMessageId already does) but I could not construct a reachable case in the time available, and a fix I cannot demonstrate is a fix I cannot verify. debt/structured-output-runname: #ROOT CAUSE FOUND, and it is neither the key nor the slot alone. Two independent mistakes were stacked in one call. RunnableBinding::mergeConfig ends with `$merged->options = $this->kwargs + ($merged->options + $bound->options);`, so ANYTHING in the kwargs slot becomes an OPTION, and `runName` is read from `$this->config` at lines 105-107. Measured through mergeConfig directly: `bind([], ['runName'=>'x'])` yields runName=NULL and options={"runName":"x"}; `bind(['runName'=>'x'], [])` yields runName='x' and options=[]. So the previous `bind([], ['run_name' => $runName])` was wrong twice — snake_case key AND kwargs slot — and my first fix, renaming the key while keeping the slot, changed nothing observable.

#upstream confirms the shape: chat_models/structured_output.ts:114 is `return runName ? result.withConfig({ runName }) : result;` — the runName key applied through withConfig, which in this port is the CONFIG argument of bind(). The call is now `bind(['runName' => $runName], [])`, which is the faithful translation and matches the measurement above.

#RESIDUAL DEFECT, characterised and NOT fixed here. Even bound that way the name does not reach Run::name(): bound directly on the model with no pipe in the way, Run::name() still returns 'ChatOpenAI'. The chain is config->runName -> BaseTracer::handleChatModelStart(..., $runName) (BaseChatModel.php:303 and :408 both pass `$config?->runName`) -> createRunForChatModelStart -> `$extra['__name'] = $name` (BaseTracer.php:282, the only writer in src/) -> Run::name() (Run.php:168). Since the model DOES pass $config->runName and mergeConfig DOES set it, the break is between RunnableBinding's merged config and the config the model receives. The loss is silent because name() falls back to the serialized component id and then runType, so a run missing its name still shows a plausible one. Next iteration should instrument that hop rather than re-derive this.

qwen/qwen3.8-27b:free: #1 MAJOR 'the hasSuccessfulWrite probe builds its uuid from the wrong last path element' — ACCEPTED, and the code confirmed it by reading. Algorithm::prepareSingleTask built the probe id from [ns, step, name, PULL, name] while the task id it goes on to issue is [ns, step, name, PULL, trigger]. In a StateGraph those differ — a trigger is `branch:to:<node>` and the bare node name is not — so the guard asked whether a task id that could never be issued had succeeded. Dead code, silently. It stayed harmless only because nothing re-scheduled a node within the same superstep. Fixed by building the id ONCE and probing with it, which is a stronger guarantee than matching the two expressions by hand.

#1 NOT MUTATION-VERIFIED, and the reason matters. Restoring the divergent probe DID make the suite red — but the only failing assertion was DocsMatchRealityTest noticing the file had grown by seven lines. No behavioural test distinguishes the two forms. The fix is therefore unverified, and saying so is the point: a mutation that appears caught by an unrelated guard is still uncaught.

google/gemini-3.5-flash-lite: #1 MAJOR 'metadata filtering breaks on non-string values' — ACCEPTED, mutation-verified. Confirmed by execution, and the mechanism is the reviewer's: SQLite has no boolean type, so json_extract over a JSON `true` yields the INTEGER 1 while json_encode(true) is the string "true", and the comparison could never be equal. Measured against stored metadata step=7, flag=true, name=p BEFORE the fix: step=>7 gave 1, step=>'7' gave 0, flag=>true gave 0, flag=>'true' gave 0, name=>'p' gave 1, source=>'loop' gave 1. Both sides now go through json_extract so SQLite applies the same coercion to each: booleans agree (both become 1), numbers agree, objects still compare as JSON. step=>'7' correctly still matches nothing — SQLite keeps 7 and '7' distinct and the stored value IS an integer — which is pinned so the fix is not later loosened into a comparison that matches the wrong rows. Mutation: restoring json_quote on one side only fails exactly the boolean case.

#SELF-CORRECTION this is a finding I REJECTED two iterations ago and was right to reject then. The earlier claim was that metadata filtering breaks on JSON OBJECTS; I measured an object filter returning 1 result and rejected it. That rejection was correct and I generalised it to the whole predicate, which was wrong — booleans were broken the whole time and my object probe simply did not touch them. A rejection measured on one input says nothing about the others, and I treated it as if it did.

google/gemini-3.1-flash-lite: #5 MAJOR 'MessagesPlaceholder coercion is overly restrictive; delegate to MessageUtils' — REJECTED, and the measurement INVERTS it. The premise is that a field map carrying only `content` is a valid message-like. Delegating would not have been wrong in isolation, but it is the other helper that diverges from upstream. langchain-core/src/messages/utils.ts:253 does `const { type: extractedType, ...otherParams } = params; type = extractedType;` and then matches against the literals 'human' | 'user' | 'ai' | 'assistant' | 'system' | 'developer' — with type undefined, NONE of the branches match and the function throws. This port's MessageUtils.php:81 does `$type = $params['type'] ?? $params['role'] ?? BaseMessage::ROLE_HUMAN;`, silently defaulting a typeless map to a human message. So the placeholder's strictness is upstream-aligned and test-pinned (testMessagesPlaceholderNotOptionalWithInvalidInputShouldThrow, testMessagesPlaceholderWithInvalidShorthandShouldThrow both pass [['pageContent'=>...,'metadata'=>[]]] and [['badFormatting'=>true]]), and relaxing it would have propagated the divergence. That makes the two coercion helpers inconsistent with each other AND with upstream: anything reaching MessageUtils directly — coerceMessageLikeToMessage, toMessage, and a chain that maps tool results — silently becomes a HumanMessage instead of being rejected. Measured: coerceMessageLikeToMessage(['content'=>'hi']) -> OK, human. Worth fixing, but it changes coercion semantics for every caller and needs its own tests and an upstream-comparison sweep across message coercion; doing that as a review-rationale edit in the same iteration as the rejection would be careless.

qwen/qwen3.8-omni-flash: #5 MINOR 'a truncated escape loses its backslash' — ACCEPTED, mutation-verified. parseString already re-emits the backslash for a stream cut mid-escape (`if ($escaped) { $result .= '\\'; }`), and the short-hex branch of parseUnicodeEscape broke that rule: `match` had consumed the `\\` and the branch returned 'u' . $hex, so it vanished. Measured by bytes before the fix: `"a\u1` recovered as 61 75 31 — 'a','u','1', no 5c. After: 61 5c 75 31. The cost is not cosmetic: JsonOutputParser's `diff: true` path emits JSON-Patch operations from the difference between successive partial results, so the string flipping from '' to 'au1' to 'a\u1234' to the real character produces a spurious `replace` for every chunk of every emoji in the stream. Silent, and it scales with the payload. Assertions are on BYTES because a terminal, and any naive string assertion, cannot tell 'au1' from 'a\u1'. Mutation: dropping the backslash again fails all three truncation cases.

#1 MAJOR 'parseNumber accepts a leading zero before a fraction/exponent' — REJECTED, half-right. Measured: `01` and `01.5` correctly THROW, so the fraction path is already enforced and the reviewer's example is wrong. `0e5` and `0E5` do return 0, which is the half that holds — but upstream does the same. langchain-core/src/utils/json.ts:128-137 is the identical shape: `if (buffer[pos] === "0") { numStr += "0"; pos += 1; if (buffer[pos] >= "0" && buffer[pos] <= "9") throw ... }` and then the `.` and exponent branches are reached unconditionally. The claim that 'upstream strictParsePartialJson rejects them' is false for the exponent path. The port is a faithful port of upstream's number parser.

audit/schema-enum-const-strictness: #RESOLVED — LANDED AND MUTATION-VERIFIED IN ITERATION 114. `enum` and `const` now use a type-aware JSON instance equality (`Schema::jsonEquals`) instead of PHP `===` and `in_array(..., true)`. #THE SWAP WAS NOT TO `==`, AND THE SECOND MUTATION IS THE PROOF. PHP's loose comparison equates `true == 1`, `0 == ""` and `"3" == 3`, none of which JSON does, so a bare `==` would have fixed the reported symptom and destroyed the type discipline. `jsonEquals` compares numbers numerically, keeps booleans out of the numeric branch entirely (`is_int(true)` is false), and falls back to `===` otherwise.

Without those four cases the original defect and the sloppy repair are the same change.

#PROCESS, because it cost a round trip and the lesson is mechanical rather than clever. My first version of the regression built an expected-errors array by RECOMPUTING `$schema->errors($value)` inside the expectation, which asserts almost nothing, and I also forgot the `#[DataProvider]` attribute so the seven cases never ran. #FIXED IN ASK.PY, and the cause was narrower than iteration 129 recorded. The text budget was `max(3_000, (ctx - 4_000) * 1.4)` and it NEVER CHARGED THE IMAGE. The architecture diagram costs ~1.5k tokens whatever else happens, and the prompt ~6.1k (measured: reka reported 6,006 text tokens). A 16k model was therefore sent trimmed-text + prompt + image and still 400'd. Worse, `ctx = next((m.get('ctx') or 0 for m in roster ...), 0)` means a model whose roster `ctx` reads large while its real endpoint limit is 16,384 skips the trim ENTIRELY — which is how 31,451 tokens were requested.

#Now the window is charged for all three parts (`effective = ctx - IMAGE_TOKENS - PROMPT_TOKENS`), the text budget derives from `effective` rather than from `ctx`, and the image is DROPPED outright when the remaining window cannot hold it. The image is context like anything else; dropping it is not a loss of capability for a review that is about code, it is the difference between a call that runs and one that 400s.

#NOT TESTED AGAINST A REAL 16k CALL, and I am recording that rather than implying otherwise — the budget for this iteration went to the fix and the advisory. What I can say is measured: the arithmetic now subtracts both previously-unaccounted costs, and `effective >= 2_000` gates the image. schema-unwrap-circular-174: #haiku-4.5 #3, "Schema unwrap silently loses nested errors on circular reference" — PARTIALLY REFUTED, with a boundary I can state exactly. Measured: a genuinely self-referential array (`$a['self'] = &$a`, verified `$a['self'] === $a` is `true`) passed into `new Schema($a, [...])` CONSTRUCTS FINE. No infinite recursion, no stack overflow, no hang. The reason is structural: `unwrap` recurses only into the keys it actually follows (`schema` for a Schema instance, plus the schema-bearing keys below it), so a cycle that runs through a key unwrap never visits is harmless — and `'self'` is not one of them.

#SO THE FINDING'S PREMISE IS WRONG BUT ITS CONCLUSION IS NOT YET REACHABLE, and the honest verdict is DEFERRED-UNVERIFIED rather than rejected. A cycle only matters if it passes through a key unwrap FOLLOWS — `properties` containing a reference to its own containing array, or a Schema whose `->schema` contains that Schema. I could not construct the second case: `ReflectionProperty::setValue` on `Schema::$schema` throws, because the property is readonly, which is a stronger guarantee than a cycle guard and is itself worth recording. So the reachable-and-dangerous half of this finding is UNKNOWN, not absent, and it stays on the list.

#THE WORTHWHILE PART IS THE CONSTRAINT THIS EXPOSES, and it is a rule the class should be held to rather than a bug to fix. `readonly` on `Schema::$schema` makes a self-referential Schema object impossible to construct from outside, so the object-level cycle cannot arise from user input at all; the array-level cycle can, and it is safe ONLY because unwrap follows a closed set of keys. That safety is a property of the KEY LIST, not of a guard, so it is exactly the kind of thing a future edit can remove by accident — someone adding `unwrap` recursion for a new key, or normalising arrays into `properties` wholesale, re-opens a fatal stack overflow with no test in the suite to catch it because the safe case is the one that is exercised. The hardening that would actually buy something is a depth or visited-set bound in `unwrap`, and that is a real recommendation rather than a fix for a demonstrated defect, so it goes in as DEFERRED with the reason, not as work.

The name reads as "keep the separator"; the behaviour is "keep the separator OUT". Both languages are faithful to each other and both are faithful to a name that lies. Had I shipped a fix on 182's reasoning I would have inverted a correct port to match my own reading of an English word.

The retry predicate is a real policy — transport failure (status 0), rate limit (429), server error (>=500) retry, and a 4xx does not, because "it will be wrong identically next time". The non-retryable path converts with `previous: $e` so the original survives, and the comment explains why that matters concretely: a raw `HttpException` escaping while every provider error raises `AnthropicException` means a caller catching that one type "misses exactly the case that matters most: the network being down", and "status 0 alone does not say the connection was *refused*". The catch-all exists because `HttpClient` is public and a third-party transport may raise anything.

#AND THE 173 INCIDENT IS VISIBLE IN THIS CODE, WHICH CLOSES A LOOP THIS RUN LEFT OPEN EIGHT ITERATIONS AGO. At 173 a CI failure turned out to be Packagist returning HTTP 502 during `composer install` on PHP 8.2 and 8.3 while 8.4 passed, and the correct response was identified as a per-version split being a timing signature rather than a code defect. That same status sits in this retry predicate: 502 is `>= 500`, so this client WOULD retry it, and would then surface a converted `AnthropicException` carrying the 502 rather than a raw transport error. Two unrelated subsystems — a package registry and a provider client — agree on the same classification of 5xx as transient, and the port encodes that agreement explicitly rather than leaving it to a bare `catch`. It is worth noticing what this says about the codebase: the failure classification that 173 had to reason about from the outside is written down inside the code that performs it.

#THE ASYMMETRY BETWEEN THE TWO RETRY PREDICATES IS CORRECT AND WORTH NAMING BECAUSE IT LOOKS LIKE AN INCONSISTENCY. The exception-level check includes `=== 0` and the response-level check does not: `$e->status === 0 || $e->status === 429 || $e->status >= 500` versus `$response->status === 429 || $response->status >= 500`. A reviewer — and this run's reviewer stream, which has produced twenty findings and zero confirmed defects — would very plausibly read the missing `=== 0` in the second as a dropped case. It is not: status 0 is the sentinel for "no response arrived", so a `$response` that exists cannot have it, and including it would be dead code. Two nearly identical predicates differing in one term is exactly the shape that reads as an oversight, and here the difference is the CORRECT distinction between a transport that failed and a server that answered. The generalisation is the sixth instance of the same lesson in a new costume: A NEAR-DUPLICATE LINE IS NOT A DEFECT, and the check is always to ask what the differing term MEANS rather than whether it is missing.

#THE PORT-SIDE BASE RATE IS NOW THREE CLASSES, THREE CORRECT, THREE ON FAILURE PATHS, and the sample is finally large enough to say something narrow and true rather than nothing. `RunnableWithFallbacks` handles the all-fail chain correctly and rethrows the LAST exception; `Await` bounds the spin when the registry empties and surfaces the rejection; `ChatAnthropic` classifies retryability, bounds attempts, and converts every failure with the original attached. All three are paths where an exception is swallowed, a loop is spun, or a registry is mutated. Zero defects in three, and the shared design signature from 213 holds across all of them: the degenerate case is handled by an EXPLICIT, STATED decision rather than by a value that happens to fall out — `$last ?? new \RuntimeException(...)`, `if (self::$driven === []) break`, `$retryable` computed from a named predicate. The code does not rely on a falsy value meaning the right thing, which is precisely the discipline 206's `if ($ctx and ...)` failed, and it is now defensible to say that THIS PORT'S FAILURE PATHS ARE BETTER WRITTEN THAN THE REST OF ITS HARSH REVIEWS SUGGEST — which is a claim about three classes, and is stated as three classes.

#WHAT THIS DOES NOT SETTLE, STATED PLAINLY. Three correct classes is not a rate, and the port has 232 source files of which the failure-path subset has not been enumerated — 211's twenty-two scanner candidates are still unread, and the scanner is still a regex. The next check should be `Promise.php:158`, the last of the flagged sites, and then the honest move is to stop sampling classes and either write the parser that makes the scanner trustworthy or accept that the failure-path audit is a sample rather than a sweep. What the three have established is that the sample is WORTH continuing, which after five iterations of zero-yield reviewer slots and three of zero-yield port slots is not a small thing to have established.

#THE PARSER WAS WRITTEN, IT CHANGED THE ANSWER COMPLETELY, AND IT HAD A BUG OF EXACTLY THE CLASS THIS RUN HAS BEEN CATALOGUING. 211's regex found "24 suspicious catch bodies". #THE ONE TRULY EMPTY CATCH IS DELIBERATE AND CORRECT, and it is worth showing in full because it is the shape that reads as a defect and is not one:
try { return json_decode($s, true, 512, JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR); }
catch (\JsonException) {
// Not complete JSON — fall through to the partial parser.

That is not a swallowed exception; it is CONTROL FLOW. The empty body is the entire mechanism — strict parsing is attempted, and on failure execution continues past the `try` into the partial parser below. An empty catch with a comment stating the intent is the most honest form this construct can take, because the comment says what happens next and the code does exactly that. Removing the catch would turn a fall-through into a fatal, which is the opposite of a fix. This is the same shape as 212's unreachable-but-type-narrowing `?? new \RuntimeException(...)` and 214's unreachable `=== 0` in the response predicate: a construct that LOOKS like dead or missing code and is in fact load-bearing, and the discipline for all three is the same — establish what the construct DOES before calling it wrong.

#THE PARSER HAD A BUG, AND IT IS THE SEVENTH OCCURRENCE OF THE 188 PATTERN — THE THIRD IN FIVE ITERATIONS, AND THE FIRST IN A TOOL WRITTEN SPECIFICALLY TO AVOID THE PATTERN. I searched in the string-and-comment-stripped text and then computed the reported line number by indexing the RAW text at the stripped offset, so every line number the parser printed was wrong by however many lines of comments and string literals preceded it. The check that caught it is the cheapest one in this run and it has now caught seven things: IF THE TOOL'S OUTPUT POINTS AT A LINE, CONFIRM THE LINE EXISTS BEFORE BELIEVING THE FINDING.

#THE RESULT, WHICH IS THE FIRST WHOLE-SWEEP MEASUREMENT IN THE PORT-SIDE AUDIT: 60 catch blocks, 1 with an empty body, and that one is intentional. Thirty-eight have a single statement, and the ones inspected are all deliberate re-throws — `throw $e;` where the exception is already ours and re-wrapping would downgrade the message, and `throw new AnthropicException(...)` with the original attached. There is no swallowed exception in this port's catch blocks that this sweep can see. That is a real result, it is the result 210 predicted would be worth pursuing, and it is also a result that must be stated with its exact scope: a sweep of catch BLOCKS, not of failure paths — a catch that catches and then returns a WRONG value is not empty and would not appear here, and neither is a `finally` that does the wrong thing, or a guard that fails open the way 206's did. The sweep answers one question — does anything swallow an exception outright — and the answer is no, with one intentional and documented exception.

#WHAT THIS DOES TO THE 210 HYPOTHESIS, WHICH IS THE PART THAT MATTERS. 210 said the port's failure paths were where the remaining defects would be, on the strength of three harness defects all living on failure paths. That is a claim about provenance rather than about quality, it explains the divergence without needing either side to be better, and it is the first explanation in this run that accounts for BOTH halves of the evidence rather than one of them.

#215 NAMED ITS OWN SCOPE LIMIT AND THIS ITERATION SWEPT EXACTLY THAT GAP: a catch that catches and then returns a WRONG value. Six catch blocks return a falsy default, and they split cleanly by the EXCEPTION TYPE they catch, which is the whole finding in one table:
narrow, named, expected          catch(EmptyChannelError)    -> false   BaseChannel
narrow, named, expected          catch(EmptyChannelError)    -> null    Algorithm:745
narrow, named, expected          catch(EmptyChannelError)    -> null    IO
narrow, named, expected          catch(ReflectionException)  -> null    RunnableLambda
BROAD                           catch(\Throwable)           -> null    JsonUtils:64
BROAD                           catch(\Throwable)           -> null    JsonOutputToolsParser:76

The four narrow catches are correct on their face and need no further work: `EmptyChannelError` is the class the codebase itself defines for "this channel has no value", so mapping it to `false` or `null` is a NAMED condition becoming a DOCUMENTED "no value" rather than an unknown becoming a default, and `ReflectionException` in `RunnableLambda` means the callable could not be reflected, for which `null` is the honest answer. That is the same discipline 213 and 214 found in the three classes checked by reading, and it is now visible across the whole tree rather than in a sample.

#THE TWO BROAD CATCHES ARE A REAL, NARROW FINDING, and it is stated as a finding rather than a defect because fidelity decides it. `JsonUtils::parsePartialJson()` is documented "Parse JSON that may be truncated, returning null when nothing parses", and it implements exactly that — `try { return self::strictParsePartialJson($s); } catch (\Throwable) { return null; }`. The value is right. The problem is the BREADTH: `\Throwable` converts a `TypeError`, an `Error`, or any bug inside the parser into the same `null` that a legitimately unparseable string produces. A caller cannot distinguish "the model emitted truncated JSON" from "this code has a bug", and the two demand opposite responses — one is routine and the other is a page. That is the falsy-vs-absent family this loop has now found in `mb_chr`, `json_encode`, a schema validator, a health-probe cache and an advisory context guard: A DEFAULT VALUE THAT ENCODES TWO DIFFERENT SITUATIONS DESTROYS THE DISTINCTION THE CALLER NEEDS. It is a narrower and more dangerous instance than most of those, because those were about a wrong value and this is about a right value standing for a wrong reason.

#THE UPSTREAM QUESTION IS NAMED AND NOT ANSWERED, because answering it from memory is the 201 failure. Whether this is a defect depends entirely on what langchainjs's partial-JSON path does with a non-JSON error, and this run has a documented instance of guessing that: 201's `keepSeparator` conclusion was wrong in the confident direction, and 207's fallback was a no-op because I did not check what the comparison did with the value substituted. So the check is specified rather than performed: in the langchainjs checkout, read the partial-JSON parse helper and determine whether its catch is typed to a JSON error or broad, and whether a thrown non-JSON error can reach it. If upstream catches broadly too, this is faithful and belongs in PORT_STATUS as a known non-exact behaviour rather than as a fix. If upstream is narrow, this is a real divergence and the fix is to narrow the catch — which is a one-token change with a mutation test, since the distinguishing test is a parser that throws a `TypeError` and asserts `null` is NOT returned.

#AND THE METHOD PAYOFF IS THAT THE SCOPE IS NOW CLOSED, WHICH IS WHAT 215 ASKED FOR. 215's sweep answered "does anything swallow an exception outright" across 60 catch blocks, and this one answers "does anything swallow an exception into a default" across the same 60, and the second question is the one that actually bites because a returned default is a value the caller will trust. Between the two sweeps the port's catch blocks are characterised on both axes — empty bodies, and falsy defaults — and the answers are one intentional control flow and six default returns, of which four are correctly scoped and two are broad. That is a complete characterisation of a specific surface, achieved in two passes, and it is a better outcome than the twenty-two unread candidates ever promised. The remaining failure-path surfaces are unchanged and still unexamined: `finally` blocks, and guards that fail OPEN rather than closed, which is 206's shape and is invisible to both of these sweeps because it involves no catch at all.
#217'S FINALLY-BLOCK CONCERN IS CONFIRMED AS A MECHANISM AND THE OUTCOME IS DESIRABLE, and the way to settle it was to measure PHP's own semantics rather than to reason about them. Three cases:
try throws, finally silent              ->  RuntimeException: ORIGINAL
try throws, finally ALSO throws         ->  RuntimeException: FROM-FINALLY     (masked)
generator that never returns (the real shape) -> RuntimeException: generator not exhausted

So the hazard is real and it is PHP's, not this port's: an exception thrown from `finally` REPLACES any in-flight exception, and the second case demonstrates it in three lines. `StructuredTool.php:260-272` sits exactly on that boundary — `try { … return $raw->getReturn(); } finally { if ($raw->valid()) { $raw->throw(new \RuntimeException(…)); } }` — so a generator that never returned produces the `finally`'s message rather than PHP's generic "Cannot get return value of a generator that hasn't returned".

#THE REASON THAT IS THE RIGHT OUTCOME RATHER THAN A HIDDEN LOSS IS SPECIFIC AND IT IS THE POINT. The two conditions that can both be true — `getReturn()` throwing, and `$raw->valid()` still being true — are NOT two situations. They are ONE situation expressed twice: the generator did not finish. And the two possible messages are a generic engine complaint and a specific, actionable one naming the tool and the cause. The code chooses the specific one, and it does so by the only mechanism PHP offers, which is masking. Read as a defect this is an exception being swallowed; read as a design it is a generic error being REPLACED BY A BETTER ONE, deliberately, at the cost of the engine's own message. Whether upstream achieves the same thing by a different route is the fidelity question and is not answered here, but the outcome is defensible on its own terms and I am not filing it as a finding.

#AND THIS IS THE EXACT INVERSE OF 216, WHICH MAKES THE PAIR WORTH MORE THAN EITHER ALONE. 216 found two DIFFERENT situations — "the model emitted truncated JSON" and "this code has a bug" — collapsing onto one `null` via a broad `catch (\Throwable)`, destroying a distinction the caller needs. 217 found ONE situation — "the generator did not finish" — producing two messages, with the code choosing the more specific. The first is a defect because a value that encodes two situations cannot be acted on; the second is a design because two messages for one situation can be resolved by choosing. The distinction between them is a single question and it is the most useful thing this run has extracted from the port-side audit: DOES THE VALUE ENCODE MORE THAN ONE SITUATION, OR DOES IT CHOOSE BETWEEN TWO MESSAGES FOR ONE SITUATION? A broad catch that returns a default almost always fails the first test; a `finally` that throws almost always passes the second. That test is cheap, it is decidable by reading, and it is applicable to every guard in the codebase without executing anything.

#THE FOUR FINALLY BLOCKS ARE NOW CHARACTERISED, WHICH COMPLETES THE THIRD FAILURE-PATH SURFACE. `BaseChatModel` is the abandoned-stream handler, verified at 191, 203 and 204 and the best-commented construct in the port — the `!$ended` guard makes it inert on normal completion, which is exactly what 191 needed. `StructuredTool` is the one just measured, and its inner `try { handleToolEvent } catch { handleToolError }` around the tracer callback is the 189 `recordHandlerError` discipline applied in the port: a failing tracer cannot kill the tool's stream. `GuzzleHttpClient` is `$stream->close()` with no guard, which is the one I have NOT verified and should not assume is safe — a transport's `close()` that throws would mask the same way, and unlike the other three the masking there would replace a real HTTP failure with a close failure. `PregelScratchpad` is a two-line restore of a static and cannot throw. So: three of four verified sound by reading, one — `GuzzleHttpClient::close()` — carrying a live unverified question that is a better target than anything the reviewer stream has produced, because it is concrete, it is a failure path, and it has an operational analogue in the provider clients this loop has been reading all week.

#AND THE PORT-SIDE CHARACTERISATION IS NOW COMPLETE ACROSS ALL THREE SURFACES, WHICH IS A REAL RESULT AND A SMALL ONE. Catch blocks: 60 swept, one intentional empty, six falsy defaults, four correctly scoped, two broad. `finally` blocks: 4 swept, three verified sound, one open question. That is 64 sites characterised and ONE live question raised, in two iterations, by two sweeps — against twenty reviewer findings and zero confirmed defects across twenty iterations. The honest summary of the port-side audit in one line: THE PORT'S FAILURE PATHS ARE CLEANER THAN THE REVIEW STREAM SUGGESTS, and the one thing worth acting on is a `close()` call with no guard. Everything else this run has found in the port is either a reviewer finding that was wrong or a harness defect that was mine.

#218'S ONE OPEN QUESTION IS RESOLVED, AND IT RESOLVES IN THE PORT'S FAVOUR — with the caveat stated rather than buried. `GuzzleHttpClient`'s `finally { $stream->close(); }` is unguarded, so the masking mechanism 218 demonstrated is structurally present: if the loop throws and `close()` also throws, the stall error is replaced by the close error. What settles it is that the author's comment at :137 shows the interaction was considered deliberately rather than missed — "`finally { $stream->close(); }` still runs, so…" — and that the stall-detection throw it sits next to is itself the reason the `finally` exists. The design is: read until EOF, and if the connection goes silent past `streamSilenceLimit`, break out and THROW a `RuntimeException` naming the URL and the limit, because "a dropped connection is a failure, and it has to be reported as one" — with the note that breaking normally would have reached `handleLLMEnd` with a half-built message and handed the caller "a truncated completion indistinguishable from a finished one." That is 118's whole thesis applied to a streaming client: the degenerate case is where the coercion lives, and this one is handled loudly rather than silently.

#SO THE RESIDUAL IS EXACTLY ONE AND IT IS NOT A CLAIM ABOUT GUZZLE. A PSR-7 `StreamInterface::close()` on a Guzzle stream does not throw — it releases a resource — so on the supported implementation the `finally` cannot mask anything and the guard would be dead code. The residual is a CUSTOM stream implementation, or a mock in a test, whose `close()` throws: then a real stall would be reported as a close failure, and the message the operator sees would name the wrong subsystem. That is a narrow, honest, and genuinely low-probability concern, and it is recorded as such rather than as a finding, because 215 and 216 both established that the discipline for this codebase is to establish what a construct DOES before calling it wrong, and "a close that throws" is a hypothetical the supported implementations do not exhibit.

#AND THE COMMENT AT :137 IS ITSELF THE FINDING ABOUT THIS CODEBASE, WHICH IS THE THIRD TIME A COMMENT HAS CARRIED MORE Information THAN THE SURROUNDING LOGIC. At 191 and 204 the `BaseChatModel` comments explained why `finally` and `!$ended` exist and were load-bearing; at 214 the `ChatAnthropic` comment explained why "status 0 alone does not say the connection was *refused*"; and here a comment explains an interaction between a `break`, a `throw`, and a `finally` three lines below where a reader would reasonably assume the code was thin. The pattern across all three is that this codebase documents the DECISION rather than the OPERATION — it records why a bound exists, why a status is classified a particular way, why an early exit is loud — and that is a materially different documentation style from the one this loop's reviewer findings repeatedly misread. A reviewer who reads a comment as a description of a live bug will generate findings against exactly this code, and has done so: 172's `allOf` finding, 186's "silently discards", 201's `separator.length`, and 216's `keepMetadata` were all readings of prose. The comments in this port are unusually good, and being unusually good is part of why they keep being misread.

#THE FOUR FINALLY BLOCKS ARE NOW ALL CHARACTERISED, THREE VERIFIED BY MEASUREMENT AND ONE BY READING WITH ITS RESIDUAL STATED. `BaseChatModel` — the abandoned-stream handler, inert on normal completion by the `!$ended` guard, measured at 191/203/204. `StructuredTool` — the generator-not-exhausted throw, measured at 218 as a deliberate replacement of a generic engine message with a specific one. `PregelScratchpad` — a two-line static restore that cannot throw. `GuzzleHttpClient` — the stream close, resolved here with the author's own comment as evidence of deliberate design and a custom-stream close that throws named as the only residual. That closes the third failure-path surface completely, and with it the port-side audit as 216 scoped it: 60 catch blocks, 4 finally blocks, and 64 sites characterised with ONE open question, which is now resolved and has a stated residual rather than a fix.

#THE AUDIT IS COMPLETE AND THE HEADLINE IS NOT THE ONE THE LOOP STARTED LOOKING FOR. Across three surfaces and two sweeps, this run has established: the port's exception handling contains no swallowed exceptions, one intentional control-flow catch, four correctly-scoped falsy defaults, two broad catches that collapse two situations onto one value, and a `finally` that deliberately replaces a generic message with a specific one. The two broad catches from 216 remain the only items with any open question, and both are blocked on the same named upstream read rather than on anything local. So the defensible statement is not "the port is clean" — it is that THE PORT'S FAILURE PATHS ARE BETTER THAN THE TWENTY FINDINGS THAT WERE FILED AGAINST THEM SUGGEST, and that the productive work in this loop has been directed at its own instruments rather than at the code it was built to inspect.
#216'S NAMED OPEN QUESTION IS ANSWERED AND THE PORT IS FAITHFUL, WHICH CLOSES THE PORT-SIDE AUDIT COMPLETELY. `libs/langchain-core/src/utils/json.ts:320-329`:
export function parsePartialJson(s: string): any | null {
try {
if (typeof s === "undefined") return null;
return strictParsePartialJson(s);
} catch {
// If we still can't parse the string as JSON, return null to indicate failure.
return null;

That is a BARE `catch {` — in JavaScript a catch with no binding catches EVERYTHING: every `TypeError`, every `RangeError`, every bug inside `strictParsePartialJson`, and additionally any non-`Error` value thrown at all, which PHP's `catch (\Throwable)` would not catch. So the breadth 216 measured in `JsonUtils::parsePartialJson` is not a port artefact, it is upstream's own design reproduced faithfully, and the port is if anything marginally NARROWER than the thing it ports. The correct triage is therefore REJECT-ON-FIDELITY with a quoted line, and the "narrow the catch to `\JsonException`" fix that 216 specified must NOT be applied: it would make this port DIVERGE from upstream for no behavioural reason and would convert a faithful reproduction into an improvement nobody asked for.

#AND THE SECOND BROAD CATCH IS THE SAME SHAPE, WHICH MEANS 216's TWO FINDINGS WERE ONE FINDING. `JsonOutputToolsParser.php:76` also catches `\Throwable` into `null`, and the caller at `messages/utils.ts:634-639` shows the contract end to end: `parsedArgs = parsePartialJson(argsStr); if (!id || parsedArgs === null || typeof parsedArgs !== "object" || Array.isArray(parsedArgs)) { … }` — upstream's own consumer treats `null` as the documented "could not parse" signal and branches on it explicitly. So the falsy-vs-absent worry 216 raised — that a bug and a truncated-JSON response become indistinguishable — is a real property of the design, and it is UPSTREAM'S design, faithfully carried. The port is not entitled to fix it, and the correct record is a note in PORT_STATUS's known-non-exact section if anyone wants the observation preserved, not a patch.

#THE GENERAL FORM THIS ADDS IS THE ELEVENTH MEMBER OF A FAMILY, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT GOVERNS TRIAGE RATHER THAN READING. A port's job is to reproduce upstream INCLUDING its defects, so a defect that is IDENTICALLY PRESENT UPSTREAM is not a finding — it is a faithful reproduction, and "fixing" it is a regression dressed as an improvement. Every one of this run's genuine refutations turned out to have this shape: 183's `keepSeparator` (upstream's own naming), 194's `LastValue` (upstream's own public fields), 201's `separator.length` (upstream measures the separator in characters too), 202's HTML list (byte-identical), 214's `=== 0` asymmetry (upstream has no status 0 on a response), 219's `close()` (upstream's design). Six cases, one rule, and the rule has a corollary that is easy to state and easy to forget: THE BURDEN OF PROOF IS ON THE DIVERGENCE, NOT ON THE DEFECT. A finding is actionable when the port does something upstream does not; a finding where the port does what upstream does is a note at most, and the cheapest way to tell them apart is one grep in the upstream checkout.

#THE PORT-SIDE AUDIT IS NOW CLOSED AND THE COMPLETE ACCOUNTING IS WORTH WRITING DOWN ONCE. Sixty catch blocks: no swallowed exceptions, one intentional control-flow catch (`JsonUtils::78`), four correctly-scoped falsy defaults keyed to `EmptyChannelError` and `ReflectionException`, and two broad ones now confirmed faithful to `json.ts:325`. Four `finally` blocks: three verified sound by measurement or reading (`BaseChatModel` inert by `!$ended`, `StructuredTool` deliberately replacing a generic message, `PregelScratchpad` unable to throw) and one resolved with a stated residual (`GuzzleHttpClient::close()`, sound on every supported implementation, residual only for a custom stream whose `close()` throws). Sixty-four sites, two sweeps, THREE open questions raised and THREE resolved — one by measurement, two by an upstream line — and zero defects found in the port.

#THE NUMBER THAT CLOSES THE RUN'S ARGUMENT IS NOT ZERO DEFECTS, IT IS WHERE EVERY DEFECT CAME FROM. Twenty reviewer findings across four batches: zero confirmed, every one refuted by a citation, a declaration dump, or an upstream line. Three harness defects in the same period: 189's never-executed top-up, 206's fail-open context guard, 207's no-op patch — all found by reading, all in code that runs only on failure or on an unusual input. And this audit's own instrument had two defects, 211's non-greedy regex and 215's offset bug, both found by the cheapest check in the run: CONFIRM THE TOOL'S OUTPUT POINTS AT SOMETHING THAT EXISTS. So the honest summary of twenty-one iterations is that the port held up under every check applied to it, the review stream produced no defect it could survive, and the three real defects in this run were all in the apparatus built to find them. That is not a comfortable conclusion and it is the one the evidence supports.

@param list<mixed> $inputs
@param RunnableConfig|null $config
@param array<string, mixed>|null $options
@return list<mixed>
The SECOND — the one a human reads first, sitting directly above the signature:
@param list<mixed>              $inputs
@param array<string, mixed>|null $options Upstream `batchOptions`. Unused by default.
public function batch(array $inputs, ?RunnableConfig $config = null, ?array $options = null): array;

It documents `$inputs` and `$options` and OMITS `$config` ENTIRELY, on a three-parameter signature. The reviewer's analysis of the PHP rule is correct — with two adjacent PHPDoc blocks the first is the one tools parse — which means the defect is invisible to every static analyser this project runs and visible only to a human, and it is the human who is misled. A reader consulting the interface for `batch()` sees a two-parameter contract and no indication that the second argument is a `RunnableConfig` carrying the invocation context. This is the narrowest possible version of the failure the rules warn about, and it is also the most fixable: add the missing `@param ?RunnableConfig $config` line to the second block. The mutation test is trivially available and is the shape the 208 lesson demands — a guard asserting that every `@param` name in a docblock stack appears in the signature it documents, which would catch this and every future instance of it across the codebase rather than this one instance by hand.

So CI DOES lint, and what it lints is SYNTAX; the style script that the project itself defines is never invoked. That is either a gap between a declared intent and its enforcement, which is a finding, or a request to add tooling to CI, which the rules say to reject. The distinction that decides it is whether `composer lint` is expected to pass today: if the codebase is not php-cs-fixer clean, then wiring it into CI would immediately redden main and the "gap" is not a gap but an unmade decision. That check is one command and it is the thing that settles the classification, so the finding is DEFERRED pending it rather than accepted or rejected on a judgement call.

The guard is the thing 234 asked for: for every method in `src/`, take the docblock immediately above it, collect the `@param` names, and assert each appears in the signature it documents. Over 520 methods it reports exactly four problems, and the one just fixed is no longer among them:

MISMATCH LangChain/Runnables/Runnable.php::withFallbacks                   @param $runnables  -> (fallbacks)
MISMATCH LangChain/TextSplitters/TextSplitterChunkHeaderOptions::__construct @param $appendChunkOverlapHeader -> (chunkHeader, chunkOverlapHeader)
methods checked: 520   mismatches: 3

So the port had FOUR docblock/signature name defects in 520 methods, one of which a reviewer found by reading and three of which no reviewer had mentioned. The defect rate is 0.8 per cent and the class is narrow and mechanical, which is the best possible shape for a documentation defect: it is exhaustively checkable, it has no behavioural consequence, and the fix is a rename in each case.

#THE THREE REMAINING ARE A DIFFERENT SUB-CASE FROM THE ONE FIXED, AND DISTINGUISHING THEM MATTERS BECAUSE THE FIX IS NOT THE SAME IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. `batch()` was an OMISSION — a parameter with no `@param` line at all, which makes a reader believe the method takes fewer arguments than it does. The three are MISMATCHES — an `@param` line that names a parameter the signature does not have, which makes a reader believe the argument has a different name than it does. Both mislead, and both are invisible to static analysis for the same reason 234 identified: the FIRST docblock in a stack is what tools parse, so the defect lives in the block a human reads. The fixes are one-word renames rather than one-line additions, and that asymmetry is worth recording because a sweep that reported "4 mismatches" would have implied one remedy where there are two.

#AND THE ONE THAT LOOKS LIKE A FALSE POSITIVE IS ACTUALLY THE MOST INTERESTING, because it is a docblock that is deliberately generic. `BaseChatModel::generatePrompt` is documented with `@param $messages` while its signature is `(promptValues, options, callbacks)`. That is not a typo unless the docblock predates a rename, and the method is one of the `@deprecated` shims that keep an old calling convention alive — in which case the docblock is describing the CONCEPTUAL argument while the signature takes the modern form. If so it is not a defect at all, and a blanket rename would destroy the thing that makes the shim readable. The check that decides it is one read of the method's own docblock and its `@deprecated` note, and it is exactly the check 216's `parsePartialJson` and 220's `json.ts:325` turned into — READ WHAT THE CONSTRUCT IS BEFORE CALLING IT WRONG. A guard that fires on all four without distinguishing them would be wrong on this one, and the guard's own value depends on being precise rather than merely loud.

#WHAT THIS DOES TO THE POSTURE 234 ESTABLISHED, and it is a change in kind rather than in degree. Before this iteration the port's documentation had been treated as uniformly excellent — 219, 226 and 232 each recorded that this codebase documents its DECISIONS unusually well, and 232 named "where the port explains itself most thoroughly is where a reviewer is most likely to find a defect" as the most reliable predictor of a false finding. That observation stands and is unaffected. What changes is the corollary: the same thoroughness has a COST, and the cost is mechanical and was invisible precisely because the documentation is good enough that nobody checks whether the prose matches the signature. A codebase whose comments explain WHY can still have comments that describe a DIFFERENT method, and the two failure modes are independent. The first accepted finding in thirty-four iterations was therefore not a subtle behavioural bug at all — it was a parameter name, found by a model reading a docblock, in a class this loop had itself read at 212 while building a probe against it.

#AND THE SCOPE IS EXHAUSTIVE, WHICH IS RARE IN THIRTY-FIVE ITERATIONS AND WORTH MARKING. Most checks in this run have been samples — four classes of failure path, six findings, two corpora — and every one of them has been revised downward when a wider scope was taken. This one is a SWEEP with no sampling in it: 520 methods, every docblock, every signature, one pass, four hits, and after the fix three. There is no remaining uncertainty about whether the port has more defects of this class, because the check is exhaustive and the class is closed. That is a genuinely finished piece of work, and it is finished in the sense this loop rarely achieves: not "no more found" but "there are none left to find in this class."

lint-script-is-a-noop-237: #234'S DEFERRED FINDING 1 IS RESOLVED, AND IT IS REJECTED IN ITS FRAMING WHILE REVEALING A LARGER DEFECT DIRECTLY BENEATH IT. The command 234 said would settle the classification is `composer lint`, and it produced this:
│ Config file created, re-run the command to put it in action. │

THE `lint` SCRIPT HAS NEVER LINTED ANYTHING. With no config file committed, `php-cs-fixer` does not check the codebase — it interactively GENERATES `.php-cs-fixer.dist.php`, appends to `.gitignore`, prints "re-run the command to put it in action", and EXITS 0. So `"lint": "php-cs-fixer fix --dry-run --diff"` reports success on a first run without examining a single file, and the reviewer's framing — "CI doesn't enforce php-cs-fixer" — is therefore rejected: CI is not omitting a check, because there is no check to run. Wiring `composer lint` into CI as it stands would be a no-op step, which is why it was never wired in.

#AND THE CONFIG IT GENERATES WOULD BE WRONG ANYWAY, so the fix is not "commit the generated file". What php-cs-fixer wrote is `->setRules(['@auto' => true])` with `->setFinder((new Finder())->in(__DIR__))` — the whole repository, with every auto rule enabled, over 232 source files and 112 test files. The project has no committed style policy, no agreed rule set, and no distinction between what applies to `src/` and what applies to `tests/`; the generated config asserts `@auto` for all of it, which is a formatting opinion nobody in this project has expressed. Committing that file would convert a silent no-op into a permanently red check, because `@auto` over an unopinionated codebase reformats aggressively on first contact. The repo was restored to its pre-probe state — `.gitignore` reverted, the generated file deleted — because a probe that mutates the working tree is a probe that has to be undone before its result is reported, and this one was.

#SO THE DEFECT, STATED PRECISELY, IS NOT THE ONE THE REVIEWER NAMED AND IT IS WORTH MORE: THE PROJECT HAS A SCRIPT NAMED `lint` THAT REPORTS SUCCESS WITHOUT TESTING ANYTHING, AND IT MUTATES THE REPOSITORY WHEN IT DOES SO. That is the falsy-vs-absent family applied to an exit code — a zero that means "I did nothing" rather than "I checked and found nothing" — and it is the same shape as the 228 instrument that reported a confident zero, and as 216's `parsePartialJson` returning `null` for "could not parse" and "there was a bug". In all three the value is legitimate and its MEANING is overloaded, and the cost is a decision made on the wrong information: here, a reader of the CI configuration would conclude the project has a style gate and does not.

#THE FIX IS A DECISION RATHER THAN A PATCH, AND THE DECISION IS WHAT THE PROJECT DOES NOT HAVE. There are three coherent options and picking between them is a judgement about the project rather than about the code: (a) commit a real, minimal rule set with a `src/`-scoped finder, at which point `composer lint` becomes a genuine check and 236's CI wiring becomes correct; (b) delete the script, which removes the false assurance at the cost of the aspiration; (c) leave it, and record in PORT_STATUS that `composer lint` is a setup stub. What is NOT available is the current state, where the script exists, claims to check style, exits 0, and writes files. This loop should not pick — the rules are explicit that style policy is a preference rather than a fidelity question, and a port's job is not to impose one — so the finding is recorded with all three options and the decision left open, which is the correct disposition for a change whose content is taste.

#AND THE BROADER PATTERN IS THE ELEVENTH MEMBER OF THE 222 FAMILY AND THE MOST RECENT ONE, and it is worth noting that it was found by RUNNING the thing rather than reading it, which is the first time in this run that has been true of a harness defect. 189's top-up, 206's context guard, 207's no-op patch, 211's regex, 215's offset, 224's blind counter, 228's missing `re.M` and 233's anchor were all found by READING. This one was found by EXECUTING `composer lint` and observing that it printed a setup message and exited 0 — the same way a test finds a defect, which is to say by not taking the exit code at face value. The 222 formulation says measurement is correct with respect to the cases anticipated, and the case anticipated here was "the script reports a style verdict"; the unanticipated case was "the script is a first-run wizard that reports a verdict it never computed". Running it was the only way to see the difference, and no amount of reading `composer.json` would have shown it, because `"lint": "php-cs-fixer fix --dry-run --diff"` is a perfectly reasonable-looking line.

#THE REPO IS CLEAN AND THE SUITE IS UNCHANGED, which is the point worth recording about a probe with side effects. `git status` after restoration shows only the loop's own working files — `.loop/metrics.json`, `.loop/packet_focus.json`, `.opencode/ralph-loop.local.md` — and no trace of the fixer. #High reasoning is NOT the discriminator. `step-3.7-flash` spent 23977 reasoning tokens and returned a COMPLETE review; `cohere/command-a-plus` spent 22169 and truncated. The ranges OVERLAP almost entirely. Truncation is not a property of the model at all — it is a coin flip in the last few thousand tokens of the budget, and a model that survived this time would very plausibly truncate the next.

#SO 258's CONCLUSION IS CORRECT AND 294'S POLICY IS NOT. 258 established that a model which truncates at 24000 and again at 7000 'exhausts any ceiling' — true of THAT model on THAT day. 294 then generalised it into 'retire the reasoning-hungry models', and the data shows the category does not exist: the most productive models in the ledger are among the heaviest reasoners. A retirement policy built on that category would remove `step-3.7-flash` (23977, a complete review) and `gemini-3.8-flash` (23036, a complete review) in order to avoid `nex-agi/nex-n2.5-mini` (23790, a truncation). That is the clearest single illustration in this run of why a policy proposed from one number is worse than no policy.

#WHAT ACTUALLY PREDICTS TRUNCATION, THEN, IS NOT AVAILABLE IN THE LEDGER — and saying so is more useful than proposing a replacement. The recorded fields are the OUTCOME (status, finish_reason) and the CONSUMPTION (reasoning_tokens); nothing records the model's TYPICAL reasoning depth, because a single sample cannot distinguish 'this model always reasons this long' from 'this sample did'. Establishing that needs either several samples per model or a provider-side capability field, and neither is available here. So the honest statement is that truncation is currently UNPREDICTABLE from the data this loop keeps, which means the lever is not a better retirement rule but either more samples per model or accepting the 71% yield as the operating point — which is what 294 measured and what this run has been running at for fifty iterations.

#AND THE FOUR-REFUTED-POLICIES PATTERN IS NOW LARGE ENOUGH TO NAME. In the last several iterations: 290 proposed recording 403s (correct, shipped 292); 292 proposed it required editing history (wrong, 293 shipped additively); 293 proposed recording permanent failures costs roster slots (measured immaterial, 294); 294 proposed retiring reasoning-hungry models (refuted here by the reasoning-token ranges); 285 proposed a spelling sweep proves absence (refuted by 286 and 288). Five proposals, four refuted by the next measurement. The pattern is not that proposals are bad — 292's shipped fix was right — it is that a policy derived from ONE observation does not survive contact with the DISTRIBUTION behind it, and this loop's habit of writing a policy down in the same iteration it notices the observation is the thing worth changing.

ask-exhausted-429-leaves-no-record-311: ## 312 — RETRACTION. My 311 claim that the exhausted-429 path was an unhandled defect is WRONG. It is deliberate, documented behaviour. What survives is a much smaller, real gap.

#THE CODE, `.loop/ask.py:530-548`: `if e.code == 429 and retry_on_429():` sets `rec["status"]="rate_limited"` and `return`s WITHOUT reaching the shared save; the `else` branch (permanent errors — 403 account gate, 404 guardrail) falls THROUGH and IS recorded as `asked`. So a rate-limited model deliberately consumes no roster slot, and the in-code comment states the reason: 'Retryable: let the caller re-pick WITHOUT recording, so the roster is not consumed by a provider that was briefly unwilling.'

#SO `retry_on_429()` returning True means 'retries are exhausted, re-pick' — the opposite of what I assumed at 311. My measured observation (no `asked` entry for gemma-4-26b-a4b-it after three backoffs) is therefore the DESIGNED outcome, not a leak. I characterised a deliberate policy as a defect because I never read the branch I was writing about, having read only the greps at :530 and :542.

#WHAT ACTUALLY SURVIVES IS NARROWER AND STILL REAL: the design trades one problem for another. Not recording means the ATTEMPT leaves no trace, so (a) the ~2 minutes burned per iteration is invisible in every cost and timing report, and (b) there is nothing to accumulate evidence on — a model rate-limited on 9 of 10 iterations is indistinguishable from one never tried, which is exactly how a permanently-broken free endpoint stays on the roster. The fix is NOT to write to `asked` (that would consume the slot and make the bookkeeping lie, as the comment correctly says) but to write the attempt to a SEPARATE attempts log keyed by model, leaving `asked` untouched.

#NOTE THE IRONY, because it is the sharpest version of this loop's recurring theme: the very harness that exists to catch 'written but never read' shipped a branch that deliberately writes nothing, defended by a comment explaining precisely why writing nothing is correct. The reasoning is sound and the gap is real, and both are true at once — which is the hardest kind of finding to notice, because the comment makes the code look finished.

#METHOD NOTE, third instance in four iterations (306 no-control sample, 311 wrong-key probe, 312 defect asserted before reading the branch): every one of these was preventable by ONE `sed -n` of the function under discussion BEFORE writing the claim. max-tokens-ignores-context-330: #330 - ACCEPTED, VERIFIED BY EXECUTION. `perceptron/perceptron-mk1.5` (ctx 36,864) returned HTTP 400: 'maximum context length is 36864 tokens. The packet HAD already been trimmed to ~40,829 chars, so the existing trim was working - it just could not be enough.

#THE ARITHMETIC NAMES THE BUG PRECISELY: 12,033 text + 1,445 image = 13,478 of INPUT. The remaining ~24,000 was the flat `max_tokens=24000` default at `ask.py:225`, which was NEVER reduced for the model's context. 13,478 + 24,000 = 37,478 > 36,864. The trim shrank the input; nothing ever shrank the output reservation, so for ANY model below roughly 40k context the request could never fit no matter how small the packet became.

#FIX: `output_budget(ctx, input_tokens, default=24000)` derives the completion budget from what remains, reserving 512 tokens of headroom for tokenizer disagreement, and returns None when nothing fits so the caller skips instead of sending a certain failure. Wired at the primary call site to `call(model, content, max_tokens=fitted)`, using the TRIMMED packet length at the measured ~3.6 chars/token ratio (reka's 40k-char packet = 11,168 tokens).

#VERIFIED: unit probe over four contexts - 36,864 -> 17,311 (19,041 + 17,311 = 36,352 < 36,864, fits); 16,384 -> 7,756; 131,072 -> 24,000 (default preserved); and an impossible case returns None. #WORTH NOTING AS A PATTERN: the existing code already carried two careful constants for this exact class of problem - IMAGE_TOKENS 1,600 charged against the window, and PROMPT_TOKENS 6,100 from a measured report - and a comment explaining that reka over-reserves so the budget should be roughly half the context. The reasoning was sound and the INPUT side was genuinely defended. What was missing was the observation that a provider counts the RESERVED COMPLETION against the same window, so the output budget is part of the same arithmetic.
